problem: Earlier large-scene simulators were either non-interactive or only partly interactive. Gibson v1 and Habitat treat each scene as a single static mesh, and Interactive Gibson made only 5 object classes interactive. Others abstract interaction as predefined symbolic actions (AI2-THOR, VirtualHome). Small-scene physics simulators lack house-scale realistic layouts. None supports end-to-end, continuous-physics sensorimotor learning of navigation plus (mobile) manipulation in realistic homes.
motivation: Tasks that need rich, continuous physical interaction with a scene, and sim2real transfer of those skills, require all of the following in one tool: rigid-body physics on every object, realistic sensor signals (PBR RGB, depth, LiDAR), real-robot embodiments, motion planners and demonstration tools. No single simulator combined them. Predefined-action abstractions hide the fine granularity of the task and hurt transfer to real robots.
key_idea: Rebuild 15 real-world Gibson scans from scratch as fully interactive, physics-simulated homes. Each scene keeps its original object layout and category distribution, uses articulated objects annotated with materials and dynamics, and is bundled with PBR/LiDAR sensors, domain randomization, motion planners and a human interface in one Gym-style simulator.
insight: Object and material randomization over class-labelled bounding boxes changes object shapes and textures without changing the scene's semantic layout, and this makes navigation policies generalize better. Depth PointGoal on held-out scenes improves from SPL 0.27 / SR 31.15% to 0.40 / 44.75%, and RGB lamp ObjectNav from 49.75% to 57.5%. The benefit shows up only with more training: at 400k steps the gap is only 0.28 vs 0.29 SPL. Virtual 1-beam LiDAR is realistic enough for zero-shot sim2real: 33% success in sim vs 24% in the real apartment, with failures mostly on the same start/goal pairs. Full interactivity lets an agent self-supervise push-affordance heatmaps; using these to gate DQN Q-values speeds up PushDrawer/PushCabinet learning, though this is shown only as training curves.
method: Fully interactive scenes: 15 homes / 108 rooms re-created from Gibson v1 scans by semi-automatic annotation. Layout (floors, walls, doors, windows) is annotated first, then 3D class-labelled bounding boxes for 57 object classes, each filled with a best-fitting ShapeNet / PartNet-Mobility / SketchFab model. Models carry CC0 PBR materials, a material→friction mapping, collision meshes, inertia, and mass from the median of Amazon search results.

Extra scenes: CubiCasa5K (6297 scenes) and 3D-Front (6049 scenes, after overlap filtering) layouts are converted and populated with iGibson objects, giving more than 12000 extra interactive scenes. These have lower object density (32 and 37 objects/room vs 75) and no baked lighting.

Virtual sensors: an open-source physics-based renderer (Cook-Torrance BRDF, Schlick Fresnel, GGX-prefiltered environment maps, Blender-baked light probes, shadow mapping) plus depth, normals, semantic/instance/material segmentation, optical/scene flow, and 1-beam or 16-beam LiDAR with a dropout noise model and conversion to a local occupancy map.

Domain randomization: object randomization swaps any same-class model into an annotated bounding box, which varies depth and LiDAR. Material randomization re-samples plausible materials per object part (varies RGB) together with the linked dynamics properties.
Motion planning: RRT, BiRRT and lazyPRM for the robot base and arm, adapted from pybullet-planning, with acceleration-bounded shortcut smoothing.

Human-iGibson interface: mouse/keyboard navigation and push/pull/pick/place, integrated with the motion planner, used to collect demonstrations for imitation learning. An OpenAI-Gym API (Environment → Task + Simulator → Scene/Objects/Robots/Renderer) is driven by config files.

Showcase experiments: SAC navigation policies (9-layer ResNet with Weight Standardization + GroupNorm, Conv1D over 4 stacked frames; MLPs for LiDAR); behavioral-cloning MLPs for pick-and-place and mobile manipulation; U-Net push-affordance pretraining whose output gates DQN Q-maps.

setting.backbone: Showcase policies are trained from scratch: SAC with a 9-layer ResNet (WS+GroupNorm) + Conv1D encoder for depth/RGB, and 3-layer MLPs for 1D LiDAR. Manipulation uses a BC MLP, and pretraining uses a U-Net (ResNet9 encoder) + DQN. The paper's main contribution is the simulator itself.
setting.training_data: RL in 11 iGibson scenes with object/material randomization: 800k steps for depth PointGoal, 200k for RGB ObjectNav. The LiDAR PointGoal policy is trained only in Rs_int. For BC: 50 human-interface pick-and-place demos (20 mug models) and 200 teleoperated mobile-manipulation demos. For pretraining: 10 random pushes × 4000 locations per scene.
setting.observation: Depends on the experiment. PointGoal: depth + linear/angular velocity + goal in robot frame + next 10 shortest-path waypoints. ObjectNav: RGB only. LiDAR nav: 1D LiDAR with 512 rays + velocities + goal. Mobile manipulation: proprioception + head and wrist RGB-D.
setting.action_space: Navigation: continuous base control via SAC (LiDAR controller at 10 Hz; exact nav action parametrization not stated). Mobile manipulation: base linear/angular velocity + 6-DoF end-effector delta + discrete arm-extend and gripper flags. Pushing tasks: an image pixel, executed by a motion planner.
setting.privileged: For PointGoal depth navigation: goal location in the robot frame plus the next 10 shortest-path waypoints computed from the room layout (GT pose/map-derived path). LiDAR nav: goal location in the robot frame. ObjectNav: none (RGB only).

numbers_note: This is a simulator paper, so the navigation tasks are the authors' own showcase setups in iGibson, not standard benchmarks. Episode counts for the navigation evaluations are not stated. The w/o-randomization PointGoal SR is 31.15% in the appendix table but 31.25% in the main text. Pretraining results (PushDrawer/PushCabinet) are given only as training curves in a figure. Per-scene breakdowns and 400k/100k-step results exist in the appendix tables but are not listed here. Rendering and physics speed tables report FPS/Hz, not task metrics.
results: iGibson 1.0 provides 15 fully interactive homes (108 rooms, 570 objects) plus more than 12000 converted CubiCasa5K/3D-Front scenes. It renders at about 410 fps for 128×128 PBR RGB and runs a full step with a robot at 100 Hz (3.33× real time). Domain randomization improves held-out-scene depth PointGoal from SPL 0.27 / SR 31.15% to 0.40 / 44.75%, and RGB lamp ObjectNav from 49.75% to 57.5%. A LiDAR PointGoal policy transfers zero-shot to the real apartment (33% sim → 24% real). BC reaches 98% on pick-and-place and 70% on mobile manipulation. The comparison against other simulators (Gibson, Habitat, SAPIEN, AI2-THOR, VirtualHome, TDW) is a qualitative feature table.
limitations: The navigation showcase experiments are small, custom setups: 4 held-out scenes, a single lamp object class, low absolute success rates, unstated episode counts, and no comparison on standard benchmarks. The PointGoal policy also receives oracle shortest-path waypoints.
Only 15 high-quality scenes; the 12000+ imported scenes have much lower object density and no baked lighting. Simulation is rigid-body only, with no object states, fluids or particles.
The benefit of interaction pretraining is shown only through training curves. The claim that partial interactivity would break it is asserted, not ablated.
